newsitem.title: JAPAN: Market sees no final chapter yet in Japan scandal.
newsitem.headline: Market sees no final chapter yet in Japan scandal.

text.p: The Tokyo stock market will continue to be overshadowed by Japan's high-profile payoff scandal even after Nomura Securities is punished for its involvement, market sources said on Friday.
Stock prices are expected to be under pressure for a while on fears that investigators will continue to probe deeper into the scandal even after the Nomura punishment is dealt.

The affair, revealed in March, has also led to the arrest of 11 current and former officials from Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank Ltd (DKB), and there is persistent talk that prosecutors are uncovering illegal racketeer payoffs by other big brokers and banks.

"People in the industry feel the affair does not involve only Nomura and DKB, but also involves some other big financial firms," one market source said. "Relations between firms and racketeers are decades-old and deep-rooted."

The stock market has largely digested the impact of the expected penalties against Nomura, traders said, since clients have already defected from the giant brokerage and it has also been suspended from underwriting government bonds.

"Of course, we are concerned about the range and the length of the penalties against Nomura. If they are much harsher than we had expected, market sentiment may be hurt," said Kenzo Doi, an analyst at Kokusai Securities.

Government sources said that Japan's securities watchdog, the Securities and Exchange Surveillance Commission (SESC), was likely to advise the Finance Minister on penalties against Nomura as early as next week following recent indictments.

The Finance Ministry will then announce penalties at the end of July or in early August, which may include a suspension of stock dealing for several months and a halt in its broking business, market sources said.

Market sources said both foreign and domestic traders have stayed sidelined this week as they worried about the widening criminal investigation into other "Big Four" brokers and Nomura's reported dabbling in shares of a Japanese loan firm.

Earlier this month, Ryuichi Koike, the racketeer at the centre of the Nomura scandal, was quoted as telling prosecutors that not only Nomura but also Nikko Securities Co, Daiwa Securities Co and Yamaichi Securities Co had made illegal discretionary stock deals for him.

Meanwhile, consumer finance giant Takefuji Corp acknowledged that its shares were probably the ones referred to in a Japanese newspaper report which said Nomura was being questioned over the transfer of shares ahead of their public offering to accounts held by politicians and bureaucrats.
Nomura has declined to comment on that report, but said it believed it was following the rules on new share allocations.

If other big brokers are also implicated, the stock broking business in Japan could be paralised, as small investors' confidence would shrink further and it would become difficult for institutional investors to make large-lot orders, the market source said.

Industry sources estimate that combined stock transactions by Japan's "Big Four" brokerages -- Nomura, Nikko, Daiwa and Yamaichi -- account for more than 30 percent of all deals on the Tokyo Stock Exchange.

"If the 'Big Four' brokers are all suspended from doing business, it would hurt institutional investors, as there are no other brokers besides those four firms that could take a stock package order equivalent to more than one billion yen," an insurance firm official said.
